title: The Food Fight: How Diet Affects Weight Loss, Chronic Disease, and Brain Health
seoTitle: Weight Loss, Chronic Disease & Brain Health: One Fight
description: How does diet affect brain health, weight, and chronic disease? Dr. Lori King, MD explains the 4 root causes they share and the first change to make.
featuredImageAlt: Plate of whole foods that support weight loss and brain health
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Weight gain, chronic disease, and memory loss aren’t three separate problems. They’re driven by the same four root causes: insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, damaged blood vessels, and an unhealthy gut. Food feeds all four, so changing what’s on your plate is one of the most powerful ways to lose weight, reverse chronic disease, and protect your brain at the same time.

title: Sugary Drinks and Weight Gain: How Soda Affects Your Waistline, Health, and Brain
seoTitle: Sugary Drinks & Weight Gain: Soda's Effect on Your Brain
description: One soda has about 39 g of sugar. See how sugary drinks drive weight gain, belly fat, diabetes, and brain aging, plus a 4-step plan to quit.
featuredImageAlt: Cucumber mint infused water as a healthy alternative to sugary drinks
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Sugary drinks are the single biggest source of added sugar in the American diet, and they’re one of the fastest things to fix. One 12-ounce soda has about 39 grams of sugar. It spikes blood sugar and insulin, sends fructose to your liver to be turned into fat, and doesn’t make you eat less later. Over time, regular sugary drinks are linked to belly fat, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and a smaller, faster-aging brain. Replacing them with water is one of the easiest wins in all of nutrition.

title: Leafy Greens for Weight Loss and Brain Health: Why 2 Cups a Day Matters
seoTitle: Leafy Greens for Weight Loss & Brain Health: 2 Cups a Day
description: People who ate leafy greens daily had brains about 11 years younger. How 2 cups a day helps weight loss, heart health, and memory, plus how to wash them.
featuredImageAlt: Leafy greens soaking in baking soda water for washing
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Eating about 2 cups of leafy greens a day is one of the simplest ways to support weight loss, heart health, and your brain at the same time. Greens are very low in calories and high in volume, which helps you feel full. They’re linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease. And in a study of nearly 1,000 older adults, people who ate about one serving a day had brains that performed like they were roughly 11 years younger than those who rarely ate them.

title: How to Quit Sugar: A Doctor's Guide to Cutting Added Sugar and Artificial Sweeteners
seoTitle: How to Quit Sugar: A Doctor's Guide to a Sugar Detox
description: How to quit sugar for good: a doctor's step-by-step plan to cut added sugar and sweeteners, beat cravings, lose weight, and protect your brain.
featuredImageAlt: Date energy balls and berries as a healthy way to quit sugar
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: To quit sugar, clear added sugars and artificial sweeteners out of your kitchen, read every label for hidden sugar names, and ride out a few days of cravings. For most people, cravings peak around day 3 and ease a lot by day 5 to 10. The payoff is big: cutting added sugar helps with weight loss, lowers the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, and protects your brain from the blood sugar swings linked to dementia.

title: Is Fruit Good for Weight Loss? Why Whole Fruit (Especially Berries) Helps Your Waistline and Brain
seoTitle: Is Fruit Good for Weight Loss? Berries, Apples & Your Brain
description: Is fruit good for weight loss? Yes, whole fruit is. See why berries and apples help your waistline, blood sugar, and memory, and why juice doesn't.
focusKeyword: is fruit good for weight loss
featuredImageAlt: Bowl of mixed berries and apple slices, fruits that support weight loss
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Yes, whole fruit is good for weight loss. Unlike added sugar, fruit comes packaged with fiber and water that slow sugar absorption and help you feel full. Long-term research links berries and apples to weight loss over time, and whole fruit is linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes. Berries also protect your brain: older women who ate the most blueberries and strawberries had memory decline delayed by up to 2.5 years. Fruit juice is a different story.

title: Ultra-Processed Foods: How They Drive Weight Gain, Disease, and Dementia Risk (and How to Cut Them)
seoTitle: Ultra-Processed Foods: Weight Gain, Disease & Dementia Risk
description: Ultra-processed foods add about 500 calories a day and are linked to dementia and heart disease. Learn how to spot them and cut them for good.
featuredImageAlt: Grocery cart of whole foods replacing ultra-processed foods
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Ultra-processed foods are industrial products made mostly from refined ingredients and additives, like chips, packaged snacks, sweetened cereals, frozen dinners, and most protein bars. They’re engineered to be easy to overeat: in an NIH trial, people ate about 500 extra calories a day on an ultra-processed diet and gained weight. They’re also linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, depression, faster cognitive decline, and a higher risk of dementia. The fix is simple: follow a 5-ingredient rule and shop the perimeter of the grocery store.

title: Beans and Lentils for Weight Loss: The High-Protein, High-Fiber Food Your Brain Loves Too
seoTitle: Beans & Lentils for Weight Loss: Protein, Fiber & Your Brain
description: Beans and lentils pack protein and fiber that keep you full, steady blood sugar, and support your brain. How to add them daily without the gas.
focusKeyword: beans and lentils for weight loss
featuredImageAlt: Beans and lentils, high-protein high-fiber foods for weight loss
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Beans and lentils are one of the few foods high in both protein and fiber. One cooked cup of lentils has about 18 grams of protein and 15 grams of fiber. That combination keeps you full, steadies blood sugar, and lowers cholesterol. In controlled trials, adding about one serving of beans a day led to modest weight loss without cutting calories, and beans have their own category in the brain-protective MIND diet. Work up to 1/2 cup a day, slowly, to keep your gut happy.

title: Is Dairy Bad for You? What Happens When You Go Dairy-Free
seoTitle: Is Dairy Bad for You? What Happens When You Go Dairy-Free
description: Is dairy bad for you? A doctor explains lactose, saturated fat, acne, and brain health, plus how to get calcium without dairy and go dairy-free safely.
featuredImageAlt: Plant-based milks and cashew sauce for going dairy-free
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Dairy isn’t harmful for everyone, but many people feel better without it. About two-thirds of adults worldwide don’t fully digest lactose. Cheese, butter, and cream are major sources of saturated fat, sodium, and hidden calories, and the brain-protective MIND diet limits cheese and butter. You also don’t need dairy for strong bones: calcium from greens like kale and bok choy is absorbed better than calcium from milk. A full dairy break is the simplest way to learn how your body responds.

title: Calcium Without Dairy: How Cooked Leafy Greens Build Stronger Bones (and a Sharper Brain)
seoTitle: Calcium Without Dairy: Cooked Greens for Bones and Brain
description: Your body absorbs more calcium from kale and bok choy than from milk. Learn the best non-dairy calcium sources and how to cook greens that taste great.
featuredImageAlt: Sautéed collard greens, a top non-dairy calcium source
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Cooked cabbage-family greens are some of the best non-dairy calcium sources. Your body absorbs about 49 to 61% of the calcium in kale, bok choy, turnip greens, and broccoli, versus about 32% from milk. One cup of cooked collards has about 270 mg of calcium, and a cup of cooked kale or bok choy delivers roughly the same absorbed calcium as a glass of milk. Cooking lets you eat far more greens, which also supports weight loss, heart health, and slower brain aging.

title: Whole Grains vs. Refined Grains: Why White Bread, Rice, and Pasta Work Against You
seoTitle: Whole Grains vs. Refined Grains: Why White Bread Hurts
description: White bread spikes blood sugar faster than sugar. Why whole grains help weight loss, protect your heart and brain, and how to spot real sourdough.
featuredImageAlt: Whole grains and sourdough bread as swaps for refined grains
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Refined grains like white bread, white rice, and white pasta have had their fiber-rich bran and nutrient-rich germ stripped away, so they behave a lot like sugar in your body. White bread has a glycemic index around 75, higher than table sugar at about 65. Whole grains do the opposite: in a controlled trial they cut about 100 calories a day from what people absorbed and burned, and they’re linked to lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive decline. Swap to 100% whole grains and true sourdough.

title: Nuts and Seeds for Weight Loss: Why a Daily Handful Helps Your Heart and Brain
seoTitle: Nuts and Seeds for Weight Loss: A Daily Handful for Health
description: Nuts don't cause weight gain, and a daily handful is linked to less heart disease and better memory. Which nuts and seeds to choose, and how much.
featuredImageAlt: Jars of nuts and seeds, healthy fats for weight loss
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Nuts and seeds don’t cause weight gain, even though they’re calorie-dense. In controlled trials, adding nuts didn’t increase body weight, regular nut eaters gain less weight over time, and your body absorbs about 25% fewer calories from almonds than the label says. A daily handful (about 1 ounce) is linked to a 21% lower risk of heart disease, and the MIND diet recommends nuts at least five times a week for brain health. Choose raw, organic, and store them cold.

title: Healthy Breakfast for Weight Loss: Why Cereal Works Against You (and What to Eat Instead)
seoTitle: Healthy Breakfast for Weight Loss: Ditch the Cereal
description: Most cereals and breakfast bars spike blood sugar and leave you hungrier. A doctor's guide to a healthy breakfast for weight loss, plus coffee tips.
featuredImageAlt: Steel-cut oats with berries, a healthy breakfast for weight loss
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Whether you eat breakfast matters less than what you eat. Most boxed cereals, pastries, instant oatmeal, and breakfast bars are made from refined grains and added sugar, which spike your blood sugar and leave you hungrier later. A healthy breakfast for weight loss is built on protein, fiber, and healthy fat: eggs with vegetables, steel-cut oats with berries and nuts, or a green smoothie. In one study, an egg breakfast led to about 65% more weight loss than a bagel breakfast with the same calories.

title: Ancient Grains: Quinoa, Farro, Barley, and More for Weight Loss and Brain Health
seoTitle: Ancient Grains for Weight Loss: Quinoa, Farro, Barley & More
description: Ancient grains like quinoa, farro, and barley bring more protein, fiber, and minerals than white rice. Benefits, gluten guide, and how to cook them.
featuredImageAlt: Mediterranean ancient grain bowl with farro and vegetables
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Ancient grains like quinoa, farro, barley, amaranth, millet, and buckwheat are whole grains that have changed little over centuries and are usually eaten intact rather than ground into white flour. That means more protein, fiber, and minerals. A cup of cooked quinoa has about twice the protein and several times the fiber of white rice, and barley’s beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol by about 7%. They make it easy to hit the MIND diet’s goal of three whole grain servings a day.

title: Fried Food and Fast Food: What They Do to Your Weight, Heart, and Brain
seoTitle: Fried Food & Fast Food: Risks for Your Weight, Heart & Brain
description: Fried and fast food are linked to weight gain, heart attack, diabetes, and even anxiety and depression. What the research says and how to quit.
featuredImageAlt: Baked sweet potato wedges as a healthy alternative to fried food
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Fried food and fast food are among the most consistent troublemakers in nutrition research. People who ate fast food more than twice a week gained about 10 more pounds over 15 years. Eating the most fried food is linked to a 28% higher risk of heart attack and stroke, and eating it daily to about a 55% higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Frequent fried food is also linked to more anxiety and depression. Baking, roasting, and planning ahead make it easy to skip the drive-thru.

title: Eat the Rainbow: Why Colorful Vegetables Help Weight Loss, Heart Health, and Your Brain
seoTitle: Eat the Rainbow: Colorful Vegetables for Weight Loss & Brain
description: What eating the rainbow means, why colorful vegetables help weight loss, heart health, and memory, and which ones to buy organic. Aim for 5 colors a day.
featuredImageAlt: Rainbow power bowl of colorful vegetables
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: “Eating the rainbow” means filling your plate with vegetables in many colors, because each color signals a different family of protective plant compounds: lycopene in red, beta-carotene in orange, lutein in yellow and green, anthocyanins in purple. Colorful vegetables are low in calories and high in fiber, which helps with weight loss. About 10 servings of fruits and vegetables a day is linked to a 33% lower stroke risk, and eating the most vegetables is linked to about 40% slower cognitive decline. Aim for 5 colors a day.

title: Is Red Meat Bad for You? Why to Eat Less, and Why Grass-Fed Beef Is the Better Choice
seoTitle: Is Red Meat Bad for You? Eat Less, Choose Grass-Fed
description: Is red meat bad for you? What research says about diabetes, heart disease, and dementia, how much is OK, and why grass-finished beef is the better pick.
focusKeyword: is red meat bad for you
featuredImageAlt: Grass-fed beef and vegetable stew with red meat as an accent
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Red meat isn’t poison, but eating a lot of it is consistently linked to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, colorectal cancer, and, for processed meat, dementia. Each daily serving of processed red meat is linked to a 46% higher diabetes risk and unprocessed red meat to 24%. The best approach: keep processed meats off your plate, limit red meat to once or twice a week, choose 100% grass-fed and grass-finished beef, and cook it gently.

title: Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices: The Health Benefits of Turmeric, Ginger, Garlic, and More
seoTitle: Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices: Turmeric, Ginger & More
description: The health benefits of turmeric, ginger, garlic, cinnamon, and more, what the research really shows, how to avoid lead in spices, and a golden milk recipe.
featuredImageAlt: Golden milk with turmeric, ginger, and cinnamon, anti-inflammatory spices
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Herbs and spices are among the most antioxidant-rich foods ever measured, gram for gram. Some have solid research behind them: ginger eases nausea, garlic supplements lower blood pressure by about 8 points, and about a tablespoon of mixed herbs and spices a day lowered 24-hour blood pressure in a controlled trial. Turmeric’s curcumin shows promise for joints and memory, mostly at supplement doses. Their biggest everyday benefit is making healthy food taste so good you stick with it. Buy from brands that test for heavy metals.

title: Pasture-Raised Eggs and Chicken: What the Labels Mean and Why It Matters for Your Health
seoTitle: Pasture-Raised Eggs vs Free-Range: What Labels Really Mean
description: Cage-free, free-range, or pasture-raised? What egg labels really mean, why pastured eggs have more vitamins and omega-3s, and how eggs support your brain.
featuredImageAlt: Pasture-raised eggs and a vegetable frittata
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: “Pasture-raised” is the only egg and poultry label that means hens actually live outdoors on pasture, and only when it’s certified (Certified Humane Pasture-Raised requires 108 square feet of pasture per hen). “Cage-free” usually means indoors, and “free-range” isn’t clearly defined. It matters for nutrition: pastured hens’ eggs had about twice the vitamin E and more than double the omega-3s, and outdoor hens lay eggs with several times more vitamin D. Eggs also deliver choline, a nutrient linked to lower dementia risk.

title: Low-Mercury Fish: How to Get Brain-Boosting Omega-3s Safely
seoTitle: Low-Mercury Fish: Get Brain-Boosting Omega-3s Safely
description: Which fish are lowest in mercury and highest in omega-3s? Meet the SMASH fish, what to avoid, wild vs. farmed salmon, and how fish protects your brain.
featuredImageAlt: SMASH fish Mediterranean bowl with wild salmon, a low-mercury fish
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: The best low-mercury fish are the “SMASH” fish: salmon, mackerel (not king), anchovies, sardines, and herring. They’re loaded with the omega-3s your brain is built from and low in mercury because they’re small or short-lived. Eating fish at least once a week was linked to about a 60% lower risk of Alzheimer’s, and 1 to 2 servings of fatty fish a week to a 36% lower risk of dying from heart disease. Aim for 2 servings a week and skip swordfish, shark, king mackerel, and bigeye tuna.

title: Fermented Foods for Gut Health: How Sauerkraut, Kimchi, and More Support Your Weight, Immunity, and Brain
seoTitle: Fermented Foods for Gut Health: Sauerkraut, Kimchi & More
description: Fermented foods boosted gut microbe diversity and cut 19 inflammatory markers in a Stanford trial. The best ones, how to start, and homemade sauerkraut.
featuredImageAlt: Jars of sauerkraut and kimchi, fermented foods for gut health
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Fermented foods like sauerkraut, kimchi, tempeh, miso, water kefir, and kombucha deliver live beneficial microbes that support your gut microbiome. In a Stanford trial, eating about six servings of fermented foods a day for 10 weeks increased gut microbe diversity and lowered 19 inflammatory proteins in the blood. Because chronic inflammation drives weight gain, chronic disease, and cognitive decline, a healthier gut may help all three. Start with 1 to 2 tablespoons a day and choose refrigerated, unpasteurized ferments.

title: The Healthiest Cooking Oil: Why Extra Virgin Olive Oil Beats Refined Seed Oils
seoTitle: Healthiest Cooking Oil: Extra Virgin Olive Oil vs Seed Oils
description: Why extra virgin olive oil is the healthiest everyday cooking oil, what the seed oil debate really says, and oil-light techniques that still taste great.
featuredImageAlt: Extra virgin olive oil, the healthiest cooking oil, with roasted vegetables
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Extra virgin olive oil is the healthiest everyday cooking oil for most people. In the PREDIMED trial, a Mediterranean diet with extra virgin olive oil cut heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular deaths by about 30%, and using more than half a tablespoon a day was linked to a 28% lower risk of dementia death. Despite myths about its smoke point, it’s one of the most heat-stable oils. Swap out refined oils like soybean, corn, and “vegetable” oil, and measure your oil, since every tablespoon has about 120 calories.

title: Mindful Eating for Weight Loss: How Slowing Down Helps You Eat Less and Enjoy More
seoTitle: Mindful Eating for Weight Loss: Slow Down, Eat Less
description: Distracted eating leads to eating 25% more later. How mindful eating and slower chewing help weight loss, plus a hunger scale and simple techniques.
featuredImageAlt: Mindful eating a colorful meditation bowl at a screen-free table
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Mindful eating means giving your meals your full attention: no screens, slower bites, and checking in with hunger and fullness. It works for weight loss because fullness hormones take about 20 minutes to reach your brain. People who ate while distracted ate about 10% more at that meal and 25% more later. Slow eaters were about 42% less likely to be obese, and chewing each bite 40 times instead of 15 cut intake by about 12%. Start with one screen-free meal a day.

title: Late-Night Eating and Weight Gain: Why You Should Stop Eating 3 Hours Before Bed
seoTitle: Late-Night Eating and Weight Gain: Stop 3 Hours Before Bed
description: The same dinner at 10 p.m. raised blood sugar 18% more than at 6 p.m. Why late-night eating drives weight gain, and how to close the kitchen early.
featuredImageAlt: Closed kitchen at night with herbal tea instead of a late-night snack
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Late-night eating works against your body’s internal clock. Your body handles blood sugar best earlier in the day, and rising melatonin at night tells your pancreas to ease off on insulin. In controlled studies, the same dinner eaten at 10 p.m. instead of 6 p.m. raised blood sugar about 18% more, and eating on a later schedule made people hungrier and burn fewer calories. Stopping eating at least 3 hours before bed helps weight loss, blood sugar, reflux, and sleep, which your brain needs to clear waste.

title: Prebiotic Foods: What to Eat to Feed Your Gut Bacteria (and Why It Helps Your Weight and Brain)
seoTitle: Prebiotic Foods: What to Eat to Feed Your Gut Bacteria
description: The best prebiotic foods, how they differ from probiotics, and how feeding your gut bacteria helps appetite, inflammation, and brain health.
featuredImageAlt: Microbiome garden bowl of prebiotic foods for gut health
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Prebiotic foods contain special fibers that you can’t digest but your beneficial gut bacteria can. The best sources include onions, garlic, leeks, asparagus, Jerusalem artichokes, chicory root, slightly green bananas, oats, barley, beans, and cooked-and-cooled potatoes or rice. When bacteria ferment these fibers, they make short-chain fatty acids that strengthen your gut lining, calm inflammation, and boost fullness hormones. A prebiotic fiber helped overweight adults lose weight without dieting, and higher fiber intake is linked to lower dementia risk.

title: Portion Control Without Counting: How to Use Hunger Cues and the Plate Method to Keep Weight Off
seoTitle: Portion Control Without Counting: Keep the Weight Off
description: How to control portions without counting calories using hunger cues and the plate method, why weight regain happens, and how to keep weight off.
featuredImageAlt: Plate method portion control with vegetables, protein, and whole grains
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: You can control portions without counting calories by combining your body’s hunger and fullness cues with a simple plate method: half vegetables, a palm of protein, a cupped handful of whole grains, and a thumb of healthy fat. Start eating when you’re moderately hungry and stop when comfortably satisfied, not stuffed. It matters because larger portions make people eat about 30% more without feeling fuller, and after weight loss your body pushes back with more hunger. A weekly weigh-in adds a gentle early-warning system.

title: Is Sourdough Bread Healthy? Why Fresh-Milled, Long-Fermented Bread Is Different
seoTitle: Is Sourdough Bread Healthy? Fresh-Milled vs. Regular Bread
description: Is sourdough bread healthy? How long fermentation and fresh-milled flour lower blood sugar impact and boost minerals, and how to spot real sourdough.
featuredImageAlt: Whole grain sourdough bread and avocado egg toast
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: True sourdough bread can be a healthy choice, especially when it’s made with whole grain flour and fermented for many hours. Long fermentation by wild yeast and bacteria lowers the blood sugar response compared with yeast bread from the same flour, breaks down phytates so you absorb more minerals, and partly breaks down gluten proteins. Fresh-milled whole grain flour keeps the germ’s vitamin E and oils before they degrade. Real sourdough has only flour, water, salt, and starter, and it is not safe for celiac disease.
